The powertrain of the baseline wheel loader shown in Fig. 1
has been converted to a parallel-series hybrid system. Fig. 5
shows the schematic of the developed parallel-series hybrid
system for a wheel loader.
The parallel-series hybrid combines aspects of both par-

allel and series topologies. In this conﬁguration, the ICE is
not directly connected to the drivetrain, allowing independent
control of the ICE regardless of the drivetrain speed. The
hydraulic pump is driven by the P2 parallel hybrid system
consisting of an electric machine (P2 EM) and a downsized
ICE. Pure electric operation is possible with the clutch located
between the P2 EM and the ICE.
The hydraulic drivetrain has been electriﬁed with two elec-

tric machines, integrated into each axle. In general, hydraulic
motors have higher torque density compared to electric
motors [26]. A reduction transmission is integrated into each
electric drive unit (EDU) to fulﬁll the maximum vehicle
speed target and the high torque demand at low vehicle
speeds. Details and technical data of the hybrid system are

In the conventional wheel loader, the operator presses the
accelerator pedal to regulate the ICE speed to get the desired
hydraulic ﬂow rate from the pump or to get the desired
propulsion torque. This brings with it several drawbacks, and
the operator interface and operating strategies for the hybrid
wheel loader must be designed to overcome them. These are:
1) Low efﬁciency in the working hydraulic system: Since

the hydraulic pump is coupled with the drivetrain via
ICE, the pump runs at high speeds e.g. during vehicle
acceleration even though the hydraulic oil required for
steering is quite low, causing large losses due to excess
ﬂow.
2) High operator workload: As the ICE drives both work-

ing hydraulic pumps, the accelerator pedal position
inﬂuences the pump ﬂow rate and the propulsion
torque. This means that the values controlled by the
operator – cylinder speed and vehicle acceleration –
must be adjusted via additional inputs, namely the joy-
stick and brake pedal.

the parallel-series hybrid wheel loader. Unlike conventional
wheel loaders, all operator inputs are forwarded to the Hybrid
Control Unit (HCU), which determines the target pump speed
and propulsion torque.
Since the propulsion system is decoupled from the working

hydraulic system, the accelerator pedal position is solely used
to determine the propulsion torque. The electriﬁed propulsion

value at a low pedal position, the operator can decelerate
the vehicle by releasing the accelerator pedal. In addition

The pump speed in hybrid wheel loader is controlled

by the P2 EM, not by the ICE in the conventional wheel
loader for the following two reasons. Firstly, the ICE is
not always connected to the pump. In full electric opera-

operations, thereby reducing pollutant emissions and fuel
consumption [27]. The target EM speed nEM,tar is therefore
calculated based on the required pump speed npump,req, while
the ICE receives the target torque rather than the target speed.

STRATEGY
The optimization algorithm based on DP-PMP requires future
cycle information, such as the pump ﬂow rate, pressure, and
EDU power.
Compared to on-highway vehicles, predicting future power

demands of off-highway vehicles is more complicated, as it
depends not only on the speed proﬁle but also on factors
such as the interaction of the power take-offs (PTOs) with
the boundary conditions. One feature of off-highway mission
cycles that simpliﬁes the prediction of power demands is their
repetitiveness. The power demand prediction in this paper
assumes that wheel loaders follow repetitive daily mission
cycles, as they operate within a limited work area, such as a
quarry. The main idea is to use previously performed mission
cycles for predicting future power demands. As described
in Section II, mission cycles are divided into smaller seg-
ments, referred to as ‘‘states’’ in this paper. The prediction
of power/ﬂow demand is based on the set of states expected
to be performed in the future.

In order to speed up the optimization calculation and make

the control strategy real-time implementable, the number
of cost-to-go calculations in the DP algorithm is reduced
by introducing a state-based optimization approach. This
approach assumes that the ICE state does not change during

not only reduces the computational effort but also ensures
minimal operating time of the ICE and thus avoids frequent
start-stop events.

Based on the controller architecture described above, sev-

eral operational constraints are inherently enforced to ensure
robust and real-time operation. As summarized in Table 2,
SOC bounds and hardware power limits are respected during
operation, while ICE start–stop decisions are constrained to
discrete vehicle state transitions. While the state-based for-
mulation reduces start–stop toggling as an outcome, it also
serves as an explicit operational constraint by enforcing a
minimum on/off duration at the vehicle-state level. Thermal
behavior is handled by restricting operation to the validated
thermal operating envelope of the demonstrator to preserve
real-time feasibility.

In this section, the DP-PMP-based control strategy is com-
pared with the rule-based control strategy through simula-
tions of two different driving cycles. The ﬁrst driving cycle is
a V-cycle repeated ten times. The prediction horizon encom-
passes one loading cycle, which consists of four phases.
The second driving cycle is the combined cycle introduced

in Section II. This cycle includes ﬁve repetitions of the
V-cycle, followed by a bucket loading phase, driving with a
loaded bucket, a bucket emptying phase, and driving with an
empty bucket. It is assumed that all future scenarios, along
with the power/ﬂow demands of the ﬁrst loading cycle and
the ﬁrst two drive states, are known a priori. The power/ﬂow
demand for each state in the prediction horizon is overwritten
once that state is completed.
The rule-based control strategy adopted in this paper shifts

the ICE torque to more fuel-efﬁcient operating points while
maintaining the battery SOC close to the target value [32].
The rule-based ICE start-stop control uses the total vehicle
power demand to switch off the ICE, with a calibratable turn-
off delay time. The turn-off power threshold and turn-off
Y. Kakichi et al.: Real-Time Capable Optimal Energy Management Strategy for a Hybrid Wheel Loader

delay time are calibrated so that the ICE remains on during
the V-cycle, thereby avoiding frequent ICE start-stop events
during highly transient operations.
Since the investigated cycle consists of repeated, nearly

identical loading cycles, the battery SOC in the rule-based
strategy does not deviate signiﬁcantly from the target value.
Consequently, the battery SOC remains close to the target
value at the end of each loading cycle.
Compared to the rule-based strategy, which is calibrated

to keep the ICE on during the V-cycle, the DP-PMP-based
strategy uses the ICE more effectively by combining electric
operation, while keeping the battery SOC around the tar-
get value through cycle-to-cycle updates of the equivalence
factor. By discharging the battery in the electric mode, the
required charge power to balance the battery SOC increases,
resulting in a shift of the ICE torque to lower BSFC areas in
hybrid mode.

the end of the cycle. Under the tested conditions, DP-PMP

Table 7 summarizes the test results for the V-cycle. The
V-cycle, consisting of 8 loading cycles, was measured four
times with the rule-based control strategy and three times
with the DP-PMP-based strategy. Control parameters were
not changed during the test; only the control strategy was
switched.
Even though the same operator performed the V-cycle,
the amount of work done by the wheel loader varies from
measurement to measurement, as indicated in the second
column from the right in Table 7. This variability arises from
the fact that the wheel loader is equipped with a bucket and
the loading phase in particular is a challenge to reproduce
consistently, even for an experienced operator. Additionally,
the V-shaped wheel loader trace may not be identical in
every cycle, which further increases variability. This makes it
difﬁcult to compare fuel consumption between different mea-
surements and to evaluate fuel consumption beneﬁts based
solely on SOC-corrected fuel consumption, which is subject
to considerable variations.
One way to evaluate fuel efﬁciency is by comparing the
BSFC of the ICE, as both control strategies aim to operate
the ICE in higher efﬁciency areas. The BSFC with DP-PMP is
lower than that with the rule-based strategy overall. In partic-
ular, the average BSFC with DP-PMP is 216.8 g/kWh, which

is 0.7% lower compared to the average BSFC with the rule-
based strategy of 218.4 g/kWh, as shown in the left side of
Fig. 20. This result conﬁrms that DP-PMP uses the ICE more
effectively by using electric mode.
Similar to the V-cycle, the results for the combined cycle

to different amounts of work performed by the vehicle, even
when the same control strategy was engaged. However, the

Of particular note is that the third measurement with the
rule-based strategy (RB 3) shows a signiﬁcantly higher BSFC
compared to the other two measurements with the same
strategy. In this measurement, the battery SOC decreased
due to an initial SOC that was higher than the target value.
In this scenario, the controller had to discharge the battery.
The rule-based controller discharges the battery by reducing
the ICE torque during the V-cycle in order to bring the battery
SOC to the target value. Consequently, the ICE operates in
lower-efﬁciency areas.
On the other hand, the optimization-based control strategy
can manage the charge-depleting scenarios, by efﬁciently

discharging the battery in electric mode. The second mea-
surement with DP-PMP (DP-PMP 2) shows that the BSFC
remains low in such scenarios. This suggests that the
optimization-based strategy offers greater fuel consumption
reduction beneﬁts in charge-depleting scenarios, such as
those where external battery charging is possible. To fully
exploit the potential of the proposed control strategy in charge
depleting scenarios, optimization of the SOC trajectory
through better task scheduling using sophisticated systems
such as a ﬂeet management system would be required.

This paper has presented a novel real-time capable energy
management strategy based on the DP-PMP algorithm for
a hybrid wheel loader. To enable real-time implementation,
wheel loader mission cycles were divided into small seg-
ments, and a future power demand prediction algorithm based
on the repetitiveness of the mission cycles was introduced.
Additionally, the timing of the ICE start-stop control decision
was changed from the conventional time-based approach to
machine state changes in order to further reduce the compu-
tational effort and to avoid unnecessary ICE start-stop events.
The developed energy management algorithm was tested

in a simulation environment, and the simulation results
conﬁrmed that the proposed strategy can reduce fuel con-
sumption by 3.3% in the V-cycle and 4.0% in the combined
cycle.
A detailed analysis of the powertrain energy ﬂow has

shown that the optimization-based control strategy reduces
losses in the hydraulic system by reducing the pump speed
in electric mode and uses the ICE more efﬁciently in areas
with lower BSFC. The test results with the demonstrator con-
ﬁrmed that the required time for the optimization calculation
is 2.2 seconds on the MABX II, proving that the proposed
strategy is capable of real-time operation. The test results with
the hybrid wheel loader conﬁrmed that the presented control
strategy can improve the BSFC of the ICE in both the V-cycle
and the combined cycle by using the ICE in areas with higher
efﬁciency. However, due to the varying workloads during
testing, it is difﬁcult to evaluate the overall fuel consumption
beneﬁts.
The proposed approach relies on correct state detection

to trigger optimization based on predicted power demand.
In practical implementation, when state detection conﬁdence
is insufﬁcient or misclassiﬁcation is detected, the controller
intentionally disables the DP–PMP optimization and falls
back to a conservative baseline strategy, such as a rule-
based controller or adaptive ECMS. This fallback mechanism
ensures robust and safe operation under uncertain or unfore-
seen conditions, while preserving the beneﬁts of optimization
when reliable predictions are available.
Future research could focus on analyzing the potential

for reducing raw pollutant emissions through reduced tran-
sient ICE operation, thanks to hybridization. Furthermore, the
integration of emission control into the optimization control
framework to investigate the optimal concept for exhaust
aftertreatment systems is another area for future studies.
In addition, the provision of future scenarios through the
networking of machines and their management as a ﬂeet on
the construction site is another research focus.

ABSTRACT Hybrid technologies are considered one of the key solutions for CO2 reduction in large off-highway machines that operate for long hours in suburban areas with limited access to energy refueling infrastructure. The effectiveness of CO2 reduction through hybridization largely depends on the hybrid powertrain architecture and its operating strategies. This paper uses a parallel-series hybrid wheel loader as a research platform to investigate and optimize energy management strategies. The parallel-series hybrid powertrain consists of a pure electric propulsion system and a parallel hybrid working hydraulic system. In this paper, a real-time capable energy management strategy based on an optimization theory is presented. This strategy combines Dynamic Programming (DP) and Pontryagin’s Minimum Principle (PMP) to optimize both engine start-stop sequence and torque split between the engine and the electric machine, while balancing the disadvantages of each control theory. To enable real-time implementation of the proposed control strategy, short-term vehicle power demand is predicted using a state detection algorithm developed to account for the repetitive nature of the duty cycles of a wheel loader. Simulation results indicate that fuel consumption can be reduced by 4.0% compared to a rule-based strategy in a typical loading cycle. Test results with a prototype hybrid wheel loader conﬁrm that the proposed control strategy operates in real-time and improves system efﬁciency. In particular, the average engine brake fuel consumption (BSFC) improved by 0.7% in the loading cycle and by 1.3% in a more realistic mission cycle that combines the loading cycle with driving.

classiﬁcation of energy management strategies developed for off-highway machines can be found in [6] and [7]. A primary distinction is made between rule-based and optimizationbased control strategies. In rule-based control strategies, control decisions are made based on predeﬁned rules derived from prior knowledge of the system, operating conditions, and empirical experience. These strategies are often preferred for real-world vehicle implementation because of their low computational effort. For this reason, existing hybrid construction machines primarily adopt rule-based strategies [6], and extensive research has been conducted in this area. In [8], a rule-based strategy was developed for an excavator equipped with a parallel hybrid system for the hydraulic pump and an electric swing motor. This strategy adjusts the motor-generator power based on the required pump power. Similarly, in [9], various rulebased control strategies were designed for a parallel hybrid wheel loader. These strategies were evaluated in simulations in terms of fuel efﬁciency and achieved a 3–13% reduction in fuel consumption compared to a conventional wheel loader. Rule-based control strategies have also been validated in real-world operations. In [10], a prototype hybrid excavator with a parallel hybrid system for the pump and an electric swing motor was developed. A rule-based control strategy was implemented and tested in this prototype excavator. Rule-based strategies are simple and have a low computational effort. However, they are typically optimized for a speciﬁc mission cycle and do not guarantee the same level of performance in real-world cycles. In contrast, optimization-based strategies introduce control objectives by deﬁning cost functions to be optimized and thus providing proof of optimality. Dynamic Programming (DP) [11] is one of the most widely used techniques for global optimization. However, DP requires prior knowledge of the entire cycle, and its high computational burden makes real-time energy management highly challenging. In [12], a rule-based control strategy for a hybrid excavator was developed by analyzing the results of a DP-based control strategy. Furthermore, DP is also used as a benchmark strategy [13], [14]. Control strategies based on Pontryagin’s Minimum Principle (PMP) are strong candidates for real-time capable control strategies. The application of the Equivalent Consumption Minimization Strategy (ECMS) to off-highway hybrid machines has been widely documented in the literature [13], [14], [15]. In [13], an ECMS-based energy management strategy was implemented in a hybrid excavator equipped with an electric swing motor. Test results with the real vehicle demonstrated approximately 30% reduction in fuel consumption compared to a conventional excavator. PMP-based strategies require lower computational effort but cannot handle discrete states, such as mode transitions and gear shifts, within their control framework. To address this limitation, the authors of [16] combined DP and PMP to derive the optimal startstop sequence of the internal combustion engine (ICE) for plug-in electric vehicles. Their simulations conﬁrmed that the DP-PMP algorithm yields near-optimal performance. Other studies [17], [18], [19] extended this approach to optimize both ICE start-stop and gear shifting for on-highway hybrid vehicles. However, to the best of the authors’ knowledge, DP-PMP-based energy management strategies have not yet been validated through real-world testing. Furthermore, their application is limited to on-highway vehicles so far. WORKING HYDRAULIC SYSTEM A hydraulic pump with ﬁxed displacement driven by the ICE provides hydraulic oil ﬂow to the valve system. There are four cylinders in the hydraulic system, namely two steering cylinders, one tilt cylinder and one lift cylinder. The lift and tilt cylinders enable a wide range of work with various attachments. The most typical attachment is a bucket used for moving gravel, rocks, and other materials, but other attach- ments such as forklift, timber grapple, snowplow, sweeper roller and material handling arm are also used for special purposes [20]. The steering system is a so-called articulated steering system. The relative yaw angle between the front and rear part of the vehicle is changed by two hydraulic cylinders, allowing the vehicle to be signiﬁcantly more maneuverable than a vehicle with coordinated steering [21], [22]. The steer- ing wheel column is connected to the orbitrol, which supplies oil proportional to the amount of steering wheel rotation to the steering cylinders in the desired direction. The priority valve supplies the required oil to the steering cylinders ﬁrst, giving priority to steering for safety reasons. The remaining oil is supplied to the open center control valve, where the direction and ﬂow rate are controlled by the spools. PROPULSION SYSTEM A hydraulic pump with variable displacement driven by the ICE forms a hydrostatic transmission (HST) together with a variable displacement hydraulic motor. All four wheels are mechanically connected to the output shaft of the hydraulic motor, enabling all-wheel drive functionality. There is a hydraulically actuated two-speed transmission between the HST output shaft and the cardan shaft. With the second gear, high-speed driving up to 36 km/h is possible.

MISSION CYCLES

Wheel loaders cover a wide range of work, and their applications are versatile. Among others, the most common and widely studied [23], [24], [25] wheel loader cycle is a loading cycle, also called a V-cycle because of the shape of the vehicle movement. Fig. 2 presents a schematic top view of the V-cycle, while the top two subplots in Fig. 3 show the measured vehicle speed and cylinder stroke during the V-cycle. In this cycle, a wheel loader loads materials such as soil, gravel and sand into a load receiver, which is typically a truck placed next to a pile of material. The V-cycle can be divided into four parts. In phase A, the wheel loader moves forward to a pile of material and ﬁlls the bucket with material. In phase B, the vehicle drives backwards and returns to the starting point. In this phase, the bucket’s position remains

almost unchanged. In phase C, the vehicle steers slightly and moves forward towards the load receiver. While driving forward, the bucket is raised by extending the lift cylinder. After stopping the vehicle in front of the load receiver, the tilt cylinder is extended to empty the bucket. Finally, in phase D, the vehicle reverses and returns to the starting point. The bucket is lowered by contracting the lift cylinder while driving backwards. The series of phase A to D is repeated several times until the load receiver is full of material.

The bottom two subplots in Fig. 3 compare the requested hydraulic ﬂow rate with the actual supply from the hydraulic pump. There is a large gap between the supplied ﬂow rate and the requested ﬂow rate, especially during phase A and phase B, as marked by red arrows in Fig. 3. In these phases, the bucket is moved only slightly, resulting in a low requested ﬂow rate. However, since the hydraulic pump is connected to the same ICE output shaft as the HST, it is driven at high speeds when the operator presses the accelerator pedal to drive the vehicle. As a result, the hydraulic pump generates an unnecessarily large amount of oil ﬂow within the hydraulic system, which returns to the tank without doing useful hydraulic work. The key to reducing hydraulic losses from the operational perspective is, therefore, to keep the pump speed as close as possible to the speed required for the requested hydraulic ﬂow rate. Another mission cycle considered in this paper is a combination of the V-cycle with short driving, as shown in Fig. 4. This combined cycle serves as a more realistic mission cycle in a quarry. After ﬁve repetitions of the V-cycle (marked as 1 in Fig. 4), the wheel loader transports material to another location to increase productivity instead of simply waiting for another truck to arrive at the loading area. First, the bucket is loaded (2 in Fig. 4), and then the vehicle drives with a full bucket (3 in Fig. 4). After transportation, the bucket is emptied (4 in Fig. 4), and then the vehicle drives the same route with an empty bucket (5 in Fig. 4) to return to

PARALLEL-SERIES HYBRID SYSTEM

The powertrain of the baseline wheel loader shown in Fig. 1 has been converted to a parallel-series hybrid system. Fig. 5 shows the schematic of the developed parallel-series hybrid system for a wheel loader.

The parallel-series hybrid combines aspects of both parallel and series topologies. In this conﬁguration, the ICE is not directly connected to the drivetrain, allowing independent control of the ICE regardless of the drivetrain speed. The hydraulic pump is driven by the P2 parallel hybrid system consisting of an electric machine (P2 EM) and a downsized ICE. Pure electric operation is possible with the clutch located between the P2 EM and the ICE.

The hydraulic drivetrain has been electriﬁed with two electric machines, integrated into each axle. In general, hydraulic motors have higher torque density compared to electric motors [26]. A reduction transmission is integrated into each electric drive unit (EDU) to fulﬁll the maximum vehicle speed target and the high torque demand at low vehicle speeds. Details and technical data of the hybrid system are summarized in Table 1.

FOR PARALLEL-SERIES HYBRID SYSTEM In the conventional wheel loader, the operator presses the accelerator pedal to regulate the ICE speed to get the desired hydraulic ﬂow rate from the pump or to get the desired propulsion torque. This brings with it several drawbacks, and the operator interface and operating strategies for the hybrid wheel loader must be designed to overcome them. These are:

the parallel-series hybrid wheel loader. Unlike conventional wheel loaders, all operator inputs are forwarded to the Hybrid Control Unit (HCU), which determines the target pump speed and propulsion torque.

Since the propulsion system is decoupled from the workinghydraulic system, the accelerator pedal position is solely used to determine the propulsion torque. The electriﬁed propulsion system also offers the possibility of recuperating the kinetic energy of the vehicle, which in conventional vehicles would be lost as heat through mechanical brakes, through regenerative braking. By calibrating the target propulsion to a negative value at a low pedal position, the operator can decelerate the vehicle by releasing the accelerator pedal. In addition to efﬁciency beneﬁts, this operating strategy facilitates one-

The pump speed in hybrid wheel loader is controlledby the P2 EM, not by the ICE in the conventional wheel loader for the following two reasons. Firstly, the ICE is not always connected to the pump. In full electric operation, the ICE is disconnected from the pump and cannot control the pump speed. Secondly, and more importantly, controlling the pump speed by the EM avoids transient ICE operations, thereby reducing pollutant emissions and fuel consumption [27]. The target EM speed nEM,tar is therefore calculated based on the required pump speed npump,req, while the ICE receives the target torque rather than the target speed.

The target ICE torque is one of the most important controlparameters that affects system efﬁciency and will be further investigated in detail in the following sections. The concept of pump speed control is illustrated in Fig. 6. The hydraulic pump applies braking torque Mpump to the shaft, generated by the hydraulic pressure within the pump. In hybrid mode, the

Low efﬁciency in the working hydraulic system: Since the hydraulic pump is coupled with the drivetrain via ICE, the pump runs at high speeds e.g. during vehicle acceleration even though the hydraulic oil required for steering is quite low, causing large losses due to excess ﬂow. High operator workload: As the ICE drives both working hydraulic pumps, the accelerator pedal position inﬂuences the pump ﬂow rate and the propulsion torque. This means that the values controlled by the operator – cylinder speed and vehicle acceleration – must be adjusted via additional inputs, namely the joy- stick and brake pedal.

The pump speed in hybrid wheel loader is controlledby the P2 EM, not by the ICE in the conventional wheel loader for the following two reasons. Firstly, the ICE is not always connected to the pump. elements.value: DP-PMP-BASED OPTIMAL ENERGY MANAGEMENT STRATEGY The optimization algorithm based on DP-PMP requires future cycle information, such as the pump ﬂow rate, pressure, and EDU power.

Compared to on-highway vehicles, predicting future powerdemands of off-highway vehicles is more complicated, as it depends not only on the speed proﬁle but also on factors such as the interaction of the power take-offs (PTOs) with the boundary conditions. One feature of off-highway mission cycles that simpliﬁes the prediction of power demands is their repetitiveness. The power demand prediction in this paper assumes that wheel loaders follow repetitive daily mission cycles, as they operate within a limited work area, such as a quarry. The main idea is to use previously performed mission cycles for predicting future power demands. As described in Section II, mission cycles are divided into smaller segments, referred to as ‘‘states’’ in this paper. The prediction of power/ﬂow demand is based on the set of states expected to be performed in the future.

This approach assumes that the ICE state does not change during each phase, and that the ICE start-stop events occur only when the state changes. The state-based ICE state optimization not only reduces the computational effort but also ensures minimal operating time of the ICE and thus avoids frequent start-stop events.

By minimizing the cost-to-go function from the end of the prediction horizon to the start, the optimized ICE state at each predicted state is obtained. In the next step, the battery SOC is calculatedby forward simulation, using the optimal ICE state and precalculated ICE torque. This forward battery SOC calculation is done on a time basis. If the battery SOC at the end of the prediction horizon does not meet the speciﬁed termination criterion, the equivalence factor is updated. These steps are repeated with the updated equivalence factor until the terminal battery SOC condition is met. Finally, the optimal ICE state for each state and the optimal equivalence factor are obtained as the output of the calculation.

Based on the controller architecture described above, several operational constraints are inherently enforced to ensure robust and real-time operation. As summarized in Table 2, SOC bounds and hardware power limits are respected during operation, while ICE start–stop decisions are constrained to discrete vehicle state transitions. While the state-based formulation reduces start–stop toggling as an outcome, it also serves as an explicit operational constraint by enforcing a minimum on/off duration at the vehicle-state level. Thermal behavior is handled by restricting operation to the validated thermal operating envelope of the demonstrator to preserve real-time feasibility.

In order to speed up the optimization calculation and makethe control strategy real-time implementable, the number of cost-to-go calculations in the DP algorithm is reduced by introducing a state-based optimization approach. This approach assumes that the ICE state does not change during each phase, and that the ICE start-stop events occur only when the state changes. The state-based ICE state optimization not only reduces the computational effort but also ensures minimal operating time of the ICE and thus avoids frequent start-stop events.

cedure via DP-PMP. DP is applied to the ICE start-stop optimization problem on a state basis. By minimizing the cost-to-go function from the end of the prediction horizon to the start, the optimized ICE state at each predicted state is obtained. In the next step, the battery SOC is calculatedby forward simulation, using the optimal ICE state and precalculated ICE torque. This forward battery SOC calculation is done on a time basis. If the battery SOC at the end of the prediction horizon does not meet the speciﬁed termination criterion, the equivalence factor is updated. These steps are repeated with the updated equivalence factor until the terminal battery SOC condition is met. Finally, the optimal ICE state for each state and the optimal equivalence factor are obtained as the output of the calculation.

Based on the controller architecture described above, several operational constraints are inherently enforced to ensure robust and real-time operation. As summarized in Table 2, SOC bounds and hardware power limits are respected during operation, while ICE start–stop decisions are constrained to discrete vehicle state transitions. While the state-based formulation reduces start–stop toggling as an outcome, it also serves as an explicit operational constraint by enforcing a minimum on/off duration at the vehicle-state level. Thermal behavior is handled by restricting operation to the validated thermal operating envelope of the demonstrator to preserve real-time feasibility.
SIMULATIVE INVESTIGATIONS

In this section, the DP-PMP-based control strategy is compared with the rule-based control strategy through simulations of two different driving cycles. The ﬁrst driving cycle is a V-cycle repeated ten times. The prediction horizon encompasses one loading cycle, which consists of four phases.

The second driving cycle is the combined cycle introducedin Section II. This cycle includes ﬁve repetitions of the V-cycle, followed by a bucket loading phase, driving with a loaded bucket, a bucket emptying phase, and driving with an empty bucket. It is assumed that all future scenarios, along with the power/ﬂow demands of the ﬁrst loading cycle and the ﬁrst two drive states, are known a priori. The power/ﬂow demand for each state in the prediction horizon is overwritten once that state is completed.

The rule-based control strategy adopted in this paper shiftsthe ICE torque to more fuel-efﬁcient operating points while maintaining the battery SOC close to the target value [32]. The rule-based ICE start-stop control uses the total vehicle power demand to switch off the ICE, with a calibratable turnoff delay time. The turn-off power threshold and turn-off

CONCLUSION

This paper has presented a novel real-time capable energy management strategy based on the DP-PMP algorithm for a hybrid wheel loader. To enable real-time implementation, wheel loader mission cycles were divided into small segments, and a future power demand prediction algorithm based on the repetitiveness of the mission cycles was introduced. Additionally, the timing of the ICE start-stop control decision was changed from the conventional time-based approach to machine state changes in order to further reduce the computational effort and to avoid unnecessary ICE start-stop events.

The developed energy management algorithm was testedin a simulation environment, and the simulation results conﬁrmed that the proposed strategy can reduce fuel consumption by 3.3% in the V-cycle and 4.0% in the combined cycle.

A detailed analysis of the powertrain energy ﬂow hasshown that the optimization-based control strategy reduces losses in the hydraulic system by reducing the pump speed in electric mode and uses the ICE more efﬁciently in areas with lower BSFC. The test results with the demonstrator con- ﬁrmed that the required time for the optimization calculation is 2.2 seconds on the MABX II, proving that the proposed strategy is capable of real-time operation. The test results with the hybrid wheel loader conﬁrmed that the presented control strategy can improve the BSFC of the ICE in both the V-cycle and the combined cycle by using the ICE in areas with higher efﬁciency. However, due to the varying workloads during testing, it is difﬁcult to evaluate the overall fuel consumption beneﬁts.

The proposed approach relies on correct state detectionto trigger optimization based on predicted power demand. In practical implementation, when state detection conﬁdence is insufﬁcient or misclassiﬁcation is detected, the controller intentionally disables the DP–PMP optimization and falls back to a conservative baseline strategy, such as a rulebased controller or adaptive ECMS. This fallback mechanism ensures robust and safe operation under uncertain or unforeseen conditions, while preserving the beneﬁts of optimization when reliable predictions are available.

Future research could focus on analyzing the potentialfor reducing raw pollutant emissions through reduced transient ICE operation, thanks to hybridization. Furthermore, the integration of emission control into the optimization control framework to investigate the optimal concept for exhaust aftertreatment systems is another area for future studies. In addition, the provision of future scenarios through the networking of machines and their management as a ﬂeet on the construction site is another research focus.

In this role, he leads the development of concept and prototype control systems for advanced alternative propulsion technologies.

RYUHEI KAWANO received the M.Eng. degree in mechanical engineering from Osaka University, in 2014. He is currently with Yanmar Power Technology Co., Ltd., where he has been involved in the development of industrial electric powertrains, since 2022. Prior to this, he was involved in the mass production development of industrial diesel engines, from 2015 to 2019, and was responsible for the advanced development of industrial diesel engines, from 2019 to 2022.

STEFAN PISCHINGER received the degree in mechanical engineering from RWTH Aachen University, in August 1985, and the Ph.D. degree from the Sloan Automotive Laboratory, Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT), in 1989, with a dissertation on ‘‘Investigation of the Inﬂuence of Spark Plug Design on Flame Kernel Formation and Combustion in Spark-Ignition Engines.’’ From 1985 to 1989, he was a Research Associate at the Sloan Automotive Laboratory, MIT. From 1989 to 1997, he held various positions in the development of both diesel and gasoline engines at Daimler-Benz (now Daimler). Since 1997, he has been the Director of the Institute for Thermodynamics at RWTH Aachen University and the Chair of Thermodynamics of Mobile Energy Conversion Systems. In the same year, he also joined the management board of FEV, headquartered in Aachen. From April 2003 to June 2023, he was the CEO of FEV Group, overseeing global operations. Dr. Pischinger has been a member of the North Rhine-Westphalian Academy of Sciences, Humanities and the Arts, since 2010. VI. EXPERIMENTAL RESULTS A. VALIDATION OF CONTROL FUNCTIONS IN THE PROTOTYPE HYBRID WHEEL LOADER The DP-PMP-based control strategy was implemented in the prototype hybrid wheel loader. The hardware used as the HCU (Hybrid Control Unit) is a MicroAutoBox (MABX) II from dSPACE. Fig. 19 shows the details of the optimization calculation using DP-PMP during the combined cycle. These results are for the ﬁrst optimization; hence the prediction horizon is the entire cycle (ﬁve repetitions of V-cycle, bucket loading, drive, bucket emptying, and drive). Upon detecting the start of the ﬁrst V-cycle at 169.1 second, the optimization trigger was set to 1. The ﬁve dots in the middle and the bot- tom plots represent the equivalence factor and the predicted battery SOC at the end of the prediction horizon for each of the ﬁve iterations. These values are updated upon completion of each iteration, with the corresponding time of each dot indicating the time at which each iteration is ﬁnished. The calculation time for the ﬁve iterations is 2.2 seconds on the MABX II, which is fast enough to be used as a real-time control strategy.

Table 7 summarizes the test results for the V-cycle. The V-cycle, consisting of 8 loading cycles, was measured four times with the rule-based control strategy and three times with the DP-PMP-based strategy. Control parameters were not changed during the test; only the control strategy was switched. Even though the same operator performed the V-cycle, the amount of work done by the wheel loader varies from measurement to measurement, as indicated in the second column from the right in Table 7. This variability arises from the fact that the wheel loader is equipped with a bucket and the loading phase in particular is a challenge to reproduce consistently, even for an experienced operator. Additionally, the V-shaped wheel loader trace may not be identical in every cycle, which further increases variability. This makes it difﬁcult to compare fuel consumption between different mea- surements and to evaluate fuel consumption beneﬁts based solely on SOC-corrected fuel consumption, which is subject to considerable variations. One way to evaluate fuel efﬁciency is by comparing the BSFC of the ICE, as both control strategies aim to operate the ICE in higher efﬁciency areas.
